tagline.text: A tongue-shaped sandbar built from coral fragments, in a protected sea

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱800–2,500 per person (per day, excluding lodging)

children.text: A coral reef sanctuary of about 200 hectares within the Sagay Marine Reserve in northeastern Negros, where a white sandbar built up from broken coral fragments emerges in the middle of the sea. In waters kept clear by a daily visitor cap, you can snorkel and see giant clams.
Carbin Reef is a coral reef off the coast of Sagay City, northeastern Negros Occidental, about
20–30 minutes

by bangka from Old Sagay port. At the center of a reef spanning about 200 hectares, a long, tongue-shaped sandbar built from broken coral fragments emerges — without a single tree, just snow-white sand stretching over the sea, surrounded on all sides by emerald water. The sandbar's shape shifts slightly year to year with the waves and currents.

This area is part of the Sagay Marine Reserve, held up as a model case of marine conservation in the Philippines. After overfishing and blast fishing devastated the sea, Sagay residents and the city government designated Carbin Reef a fish sanctuary in the
; a presidential proclamation placed a wide stretch of water under protection in
, and in
, Republic Act 9106 codified about 32,000 hectares of the sea off Sagay City as a "Protected Seascape." As a result, coral and fish have rebounded, and the area now even runs a giant clam sanctuary.

Tourism here is run jointly with the local community. Visitors must register at the tourism office in Old Sagay and hire a boat from the local boat association, and snorkeling guides are drawn from local fishermen. To protect the area, daily visitor numbers are capped, and camping on the sandbar is not allowed.

Rather than expecting a resort or amenities, come here to see a clean sandbar and a revived coral reef in an uncrowded sea. Combining it with the nearby Suyac Island Mangrove Eco-Park lets you see coral reef, mangroves, and a bat roost all in one trip, making it a good nature-study outing for kids too.

blocks.title: Walking the sandbar on the open sea

children.text: Walk the white, coral-fragment sandbar from one end to the other. The water's shifting layers of color on either side are striking, and a drone or elevated shot best captures its tongue shape.
Get in the water at the reef edge along the sandbar with a local snorkeling guide. You can see hard and soft coral, clownfish, butterflyfish, and parrotfish in shallow depths.
See giant clams (taklobo) raised within the protected area. The blue and purple mantles visible between their shells are beautiful, but never touch or step on them.
A small island close to Carbin Reef, where you can walk the mangrove forest along a roughly
bamboo boardwalk and go kayaking. You can also see thousands of fruit bats roosting in the trees.

blocks.title: The sea view from the watchtower

children.text: A watchtower and hut guarding the protected area stand near the sandbar, letting you look down from height over the reef's boundary and the whole sandbar.

Molocaboc Island, within the protected area, is a fishing village where wooden walkways over the water link the houses. You can stop by for an extra boat fee and get a glimpse of residents' life on the sea.
Kinilaw, freshly caught fish tossed in vinegar, ginger, and chili, is Sagay's coastal signature dish. Ask at a restaurant near the port or your boatman to try fresh seafood.

The
December–May
dry season is good, and
March–May
especially, when the winds die down, brings the calmest sea and the best underwater visibility, ideal for snorkeling. Through
June
, dry days often continue as well. During
December–February
, on the other hand, the northeast monsoon can raise waves on some days, making the boat ride rougher.
July–November

is the wet season and typhoon period; the water turns murky on cloudy days, and boat service stops when a typhoon signal is raised. The sandbar is widest at low tide, so the tide on the day of your visit matters more than the season. With almost no shade at midday, even a temperature of
can feel much hotter than it sounds.

There's no lodging on the Carbin Reef sandbar, and camping is prohibited. Sagay town has small hotels and pensions at about

a night, and it's convenient to stay in Sagay the night before if you want to catch an early boat. If you want lodging with more amenities, you can stay in Bacolod and take a pre-dawn bus, or stay at a resort on Lakawon Island and split your visit over two days. Suyac Island also has nipa huts, but you'll need to check with the tourism office whether overnight stays are offered.

Sagay is a city blending fishing villages and sugarcane farms, so seafood is fresh and cheap. Fish kinilaw tossed with vinegar, ginger, onion, and chili, charcoal-grilled fish and squid, and tangy sinigang soup are the signature dishes, and being in northern Negros, chicken inasal restaurants are easy to find too. There are no shops on the sandbar, so be sure to buy water and simple snacks in Sagay before heading out, and take all your trash back with you.
Daily visitor numbers are capped at around 100, and some slots are reserved in advance. On weekends and during peak season, book ahead with the Sagay tourism office by phone or email.
Check the tide chart and arrive at low tide for the sandbar at its widest and most vivid.
The sandbar has almost no shade. A rash guard, a wide-brimmed hat, sunglasses, and reef-safe sunscreen are essential.
The sand is made of coral fragments, so it's uncomfortable to walk barefoot. Aqua shoes make both the sandbar walk and snorkeling more comfortable.
Snorkel with a local guide. They'll point out where currents pick up and where the coral is fragile.
Cell signal tends to be weak, so arrange your return transport and meeting time in advance.
Traveling alone makes the boat fare a heavier burden, so ask when registering whether you can share a boat with other travelers.
The last bus from Sagay bus terminal to Bacolod sometimes stops running before evening, so return to the terminal by mid-afternoon at the latest.

Carbin Reef is a legally protected marine sanctuary. Touching or taking coral, shells, or starfish, camping on the sandbar, and littering are all prohibited, and violations can incur fines. Booking and fee rules change often, so check the Sagay tourism office's latest notices.
While snorkeling, stay floating on the surface so you don't stand on coral or kick it with your fins.
Wear a life jacket in the edge channels where currents get strong, regardless of your swimming ability.
Boats don't run when there's a typhoon signal or a strong wind forecast. Postpone your trip if the weather is bad.
The sandbar narrows quickly as the tide comes in. Don't leave belongings near the water's edge, and follow your boatman's instructions on when to head back.
With no shade, the risk of heatstroke and dehydration is high. Bring at least 1.5L of water per person.
